selectedCourses.name: Personal & Professional Development
selectedCourses.evidenceRead: Develops academic writing and research-literacy skills alongside personal development and civic engagement. Students locate and evaluate scholarly sources, synthesize literature, formulate research questions and arguments, and construct a research-paper introduction. A community-engaged project with a societal partner connects these skills to collaboration, reflection and practical contribution. Personal development planning addresses learning goals, self-efficacy, and stress and time management; the course also considers responsible academic use of AI.
selectedCourses.officialDescriptionRead: This course is a first-year requirement and aims to stimulate personal development, namely, being able to actively, consciously and ethically orientate oneself in relation to others and the world. It supports the development of core personal and academic skills that enhance critical thinking and independent learning. It seeks to improve and develop academic writing and presenting skills and helps students develop the foundational skills and attitudes to reflect on societal issues and engage with societal partners.
selectedCourses.contribution: First-year academic writing, research literacy, personal development and civic engagement.
selectedCourses.descriptionRead: This course is a first-year requirement and aims to stimulate personal development, namely, being able to actively, consciously and ethically orientate oneself in relation to others and the world. It supports the development of core personal and academic skills that enhance critical thinking and independent learning. It seeks to improve and develop academic writing and presenting skills and helps students develop the foundational skills and attitudes to reflect on societal issues and engage with societal partners.

selectedCourses.name: AI Ethics
selectedCourses.evidenceRead: Examines AI through ethical theory and psychological accounts of human behaviour and interaction. Ethical debates address fairness, privacy, responsibility, alignment, moral status and political or existential risks. Psychological perspectives consider development, clinical care, social and organizational relationships, forensic applications and cognitive neuroscience. Students synthesize literature and apply ethical frameworks in an analytical psychology project and a research-grounded podcast, with a creative communication component.
selectedCourses.officialDescriptionRead: Explores philosophical foundations and implications of AI. Examines the history of AI, ethical issues like interpretability, bias and alignment, debates about AI consciousness and implications for human nature.
selectedCourses.contribution: Examines fairness, privacy, responsibility, alignment, moral status and political risks through ethical theory and psychological perspectives, with a literature-based project and podcast. Directly contributes AI ethics; interpretability or a specialised philosophy-of-information syllabus is not assumed.
selectedCourses.descriptionRead: AI Ethics examines artificial intelligence from philosophical and psychological perspectives. Topics include fairness, privacy, responsibility, human-value alignment, moral status and political or existential risks. Students apply ethical frameworks to questions about human behaviour and interaction, synthesise research in an analytical psychology project, and produce a research-based podcast.

selectedCourses.name: Logic & Discrete Mathematics
selectedCourses.evidenceRead: Introduces formal logic, abstract mathematical reasoning and proof. Students analyze propositions and quantified statements, work with sets, Boolean algebra, functions and relations, and develop direct and indirect proofs. Induction and recursive definitions extend these tools to mathematical structures. The final component systematically models processes and games without chance and investigates the existence and construction of winning strategies.
selectedCourses.officialDescriptionRead: Focuses on mathematics of decision‑making, covering topics in discrete mathematics such as logic, patterns and structures, with applications to computer science and algorithm construction.
selectedCourses.contribution: Develops propositional and quantified logic, proof, sets, Boolean algebra, functions, induction and recursion, then formal modelling of games without chance. Directly supports logical argument; mathematical applications complement philosophical reasoning.
selectedCourses.descriptionRead: Focuses on mathematics of decision‑making, covering topics in discrete mathematics such as logic, patterns and structures, with applications to computer science and algorithm construction.

selectedCourses.name: Database Management Systems
selectedCourses.evidenceRead: Introduces relational database management systems and SQL. Covers relational database theory, authorization, normalization and query processing.
selectedCourses.officialDescriptionRead: Introduces relational database management systems and SQL. Covers relational database theory, authorization, normalization and query processing.
selectedCourses.contribution: examines how information is modelled, structured, stored and queried, which is the concrete substance behind philosophical claims about information and computation
selectedCourses.descriptionRead: Introduces relational database management systems and SQL. Covers relational database theory, authorization, normalization and query processing.

selectedCourses.name: Introduction to Data Science
selectedCourses.evidenceRead: Introduces data analysis and visualization in R through practical work with tabular, textual and spatial data. Students import, clean, transform and join data, explore patterns, and construct visualizations using tidy-data principles and the grammar of graphics. Web scraping and basic programming functions extend the workflow. A student research project applies these tools to a question using data from a field of interest.
selectedCourses.officialDescriptionRead: Develops foundational skills in data visualization, cleaning and manipulation. Explores spatial and text data and includes hands‑on work with datasets from various disciplines.
selectedCourses.contribution: introduces data practice and the computational handling of information that a philosophy of information has to engage with concretely
selectedCourses.descriptionRead: Develops foundational skills in data visualization, cleaning and manipulation. Explores spatial and text data and includes hands‑on work with datasets from various disciplines.

selectedCourses.name: Machine Learning
selectedCourses.evidenceRead: Introduces statistical learning for understanding data and predicting outcomes. Students study regression and classification, model accuracy, resampling, regularization, nonlinear models, trees, support vector machines and unsupervised learning. Practical assignments evaluate methods on real data using R or Python. Projects emphasize informative predictor construction, test-set prediction, appropriate model choice and clear reporting of results and limitations.
selectedCourses.officialDescriptionRead: Covers core machine learning techniques from linear regression to advanced tree‑based methods. Discusses strengths and weaknesses and applies methods to real data from fields like medicine, physics and economics.
selectedCourses.contribution: provides working knowledge of the machine-learning models whose behaviour and limits the programme evaluates
selectedCourses.descriptionRead: Machine Learning introduces methods for understanding data and making predictions, including linear regression, classification, resampling, shrinkage, tree-based methods, support vector machines and clustering. Real-world examples illustrate the methods, their strengths and limitations.

sharedDescriptionProvenance.reviewNote: Compared with the current selected workbook field. Retained the existing description as a faithful account; updated its source provenance.

selectedCourses.name: Neural Networks & Deep Learning
selectedCourses.evidenceRead: Develops neural-network theory and practical implementation in Python, Keras and TensorFlow. Students build and train simple networks before studying multilayer architectures, backpropagation, regularization and model evaluation. Later work applies deep learning to computer vision, time series and text, including transformers. Projects construct predictors for tabular data and investigate an independently chosen image- or text-based prediction problem, with experimental results reported in a paper.
selectedCourses.officialDescriptionRead: Explores theory and practice of neural networks. Students build basic networks and progress to complex networks for computer vision, and discuss recent developments in large language and image generation models.
selectedCourses.contribution: examines neural network architectures and deep learning, the specific technology behind current claims about artificial intelligence
selectedCourses.descriptionRead: Neural Networks & Deep Learning combines theory with practical Python, Keras and TensorFlow implementations. Students build and train networks, study backpropagation, regularisation and model evaluation, and apply deep learning to computer vision, time series and text, including transformers. Projects investigate prediction problems and report experimental results.

sharedDescriptionProvenance.reviewNote: Compared with the current selected workbook field. Revised the description to retain supported academic scope and activities without superseded or unsupported details.

selectedCourses.name: Mathematical Methods
selectedCourses.evidenceRead: Develops single-variable calculus and related mathematical tools for modelling scientific problems. Functions, limits and differentiation lead to optimization, Taylor series, complex numbers, integration and differential equations. Students solve problems analytically and with Mathematica, including numerical approximation. A project implements, analyzes and adapts a dynamic model, requiring interpretation of its behaviour and explanation of the computational results.
selectedCourses.officialDescriptionRead: Introduces linear algebra (vectors, matrices, eigenvalues) and calculus (limits, differentiation, integration) to construct and solve equations. Provides problem‑solving skills applicable across disciplines.
selectedCourses.contribution: supplies the mathematical methods required for the later formal and machine-learning work
selectedCourses.descriptionRead: Mathematical Methods develops foundational techniques in differentiation, integration, complex numbers and differential equations. Students solve problems analytically and with Mathematica. A project implements, analyses and adapts a dynamic model, requiring interpretation of its behaviour and computational results.

sharedDescriptionProvenance.reviewNote: Compared with the current selected workbook field. Revised the description to retain supported academic scope and activities without superseded or unsupported details.

selectedCourses.name: R3: Recycling, Recovery, Remediation
selectedCourses.evidenceRead: Studies resource circularity through solar-panel recycling, metal recovery from electronic waste, and soil remediation using plants and mycelium. Theory and extensive laboratory work connect material composition and separation technologies to resource yields, environmental consequences and recycling constraints. Students develop leaching protocols, analyze metal concentrations and recovery, cultivate fungal networks, and use microscopy to characterize materials and mycelium growth.
selectedCourses.officialDescriptionRead: Examines strategies and technologies towards a circular economy. Explores resource security and stewardship, develops lab skills and inorganic chemistry knowledge, and connects to themes at the Delta Climate Center.
selectedCourses.contribution: examines recycling, recovery and remediation as material responses to environmental harm
selectedCourses.descriptionRead: Examines strategies and technologies towards a circular economy. Explores resource security and stewardship, develops lab skills and inorganic chemistry knowledge, and connects to themes at the Delta Climate Center.

selectedCourses.name: Governance of Sustainability
selectedCourses.evidenceRead: Analyzes sustainability as a problem of collective decision-making involving governments, markets and civil society. Concepts of institutions, power, participation, justice and problem complexity frame competing technological and systemic responses. Structured cases examine food, freshwater, energy and climate mitigation. Students apply governance frameworks to a Zeeland issue, consult relevant organizations or experts, and produce policy advice or an evaluation assessing effectiveness, feasibility and stakeholder interests.
selectedCourses.officialDescriptionRead: This course examines sustainability through the lens of governance: “a process of rule-making and collective decision-making that includes both governmental and non-governmental actors in shaping public policy” (Fenger & Bekkers, 2016). Taking this lens, we ask questions such as how are sustainability policies on the local, national, and international level made and enforced? Which actors represent which interests, and which are most influential? How is public opinion on sustainability shaped, and how does public opinion shape politics? What, at the end of the day, determines effective policy for sustainability? By the end of this course, you will have gained a deep appreciation of the complexity of the governance dimension of sustainability, and have developed the theoretical and practical understanding to critically assess mainstream policy decisions.
selectedCourses.contribution: analyses how sustainability is governed, regulated and contested across institutions
selectedCourses.descriptionRead: This course examines sustainability through the lens of governance: “a process of rule-making and collective decision-making that includes both governmental and non-governmental actors in shaping public policy” (Fenger & Bekkers, 2016). Taking this lens, we ask questions such as how are sustainability policies on the local, national, and international level made and enforced? Which actors represent which interests, and which are most influential? How is public opinion on sustainability shaped, and how does public opinion shape politics? What, at the end of the day, determines effective policy for sustainability? By the end of this course, you will have gained a deep appreciation of the complexity of the governance dimension of sustainability, and have developed the theoretical and practical understanding to critically assess mainstream policy decisions.

selectedCourses.name: Ecosystems Uncovered: How Nature Works
selectedCourses.evidenceRead: Develops ecological principles from organisms and populations to communities and ecosystems. Environmental conditions, resources and life cycles frame competition, feeding relationships, selection, population dynamics and biodiversity. Energy and matter cycles connect ecological processes to conservation and human impacts. Dedicated practical sessions teach simple ecological modelling in R, and a small research project communicates findings through a poster.
selectedCourses.officialDescriptionRead: Focuses on basic principles of ecology. Studies how environmental conditions affect organisms and examines ecological principles governing individuals, populations, communities and ecosystems, including ecological modelling and applied case studies.
selectedCourses.contribution: explains how ecosystems function, which the value claims made about nature presuppose
selectedCourses.descriptionRead: Focuses on basic principles of ecology. Studies how environmental conditions affect organisms and examines ecological principles governing individuals, populations, communities and ecosystems, including ecological modelling and applied case studies.

selectedCourses.name: Earth's Resources
selectedCourses.evidenceRead: Provides in‑depth geoscience research into resource and environmental challenges such as nuclear waste storage, geothermal energy and CO₂ capture. Students conduct literature reviews and produce class reports for presentation to a professional conference.
selectedCourses.officialDescriptionRead: Provides in‑depth geoscience research into resource and environmental challenges such as nuclear waste storage, geothermal energy and CO₂ capture. Students conduct literature reviews and produce class reports for presentation to a professional conference.
selectedCourses.contribution: Investigates nuclear waste storage, geothermal energy and CO2 capture through geoscience literature research, class reports and a professional-conference presentation. These resource and environmental cases give concrete scientific constraints for environmental responsibility; no dedicated theory of resource justice is assumed.
selectedCourses.descriptionRead: Provides in‑depth geoscience research into resource and environmental challenges such as nuclear waste storage, geothermal energy and CO₂ capture. Students conduct literature reviews and produce class reports for presentation to a professional conference.

selectedCourses.name: Sustainability Essentials I
selectedCourses.evidenceRead: Uses planetary boundaries to introduce scientific tools for understanding sustainability and human impacts on Earth systems. Students interpret graphs and uncertainty, build simple dynamic models, and learn chemical, thermodynamic and mechanical principles relevant to environmental processes. Topics connect climate, ocean acidification, nutrient cycles, energy and materials. An iterative laboratory project makes starch-based biopolymers and measures their strength and elasticity to improve the formulation.
selectedCourses.officialDescriptionRead: Provides key concepts in physics, chemistry, materials science, mathematics and modelling necessary for sustainability. Uses a case study to connect concepts to real‑world sustainability challenges and prepares students for 200‑level sustainability courses.
selectedCourses.contribution: Introduces planetary boundaries, physical and chemical sustainability processes, uncertainty and dynamic models, with a biopolymer laboratory project. Provides concrete environmental-science foundations for evaluating sustainability claims.
selectedCourses.descriptionRead: Introduces sustainability through planetary boundaries and scientific tools for understanding human impacts on Earth systems. Students interpret graphs and uncertainty, build simple dynamic models, and study chemical and physical principles relevant to climate, energy and materials. A laboratory project makes and tests starch-based biopolymers.

selectedCourses.name: Sustainability Essentials II
selectedCourses.evidenceRead: Connects wave physics, chemistry and materials science to sustainability questions. Students study wave behaviour and observation methods, chemical analysis, microscopic material structure and macroscopic stress and strain. Practical sessions include wave applications and chemistry laboratory work. Reflective inquiries and a final project critically assess sustainability campaigns, identify greenwashing and communicate evidence-based improvements to a public audience.
selectedCourses.officialDescriptionRead: Builds on Sustainability Essentials I. Applies tools and knowledge to a real‑world sustainability case study and allows students to delve deeper into aspects connected to their field of interest.
selectedCourses.contribution: Develops wave physics, chemical analysis and material properties, with laboratory work and critical assessment of sustainability campaigns and greenwashing. It supplies scientific and evaluative tools for the environmental-practice concept.
selectedCourses.descriptionRead: Develops physical-science foundations for sustainability through waves, chemistry and materials science. Reflective work and a project apply these topics to analysing greenwashing.

selectedCourses.name: Climate Change
selectedCourses.evidenceRead: Introduces climate-change science, societal impacts, and mitigation and adaptation. Students examine greenhouse gases, feedbacks, tipping points, ocean acidification and sea-level rise, then consequences for ecosystems, agriculture, transport, buildings and health. Climate justice, governance, communication and misinformation connect physical changes to social responses. Solution pathways include energy systems, carbon removal and climate-adaptive planning. Students interview a stakeholder and produce a short film, alongside reflection on their own role.
selectedCourses.officialDescriptionRead: Focuses on drivers and impacts of anthropogenic climate change on sea level, ocean acidification, ecology and society. Discusses adaptation and mitigation solutions, including renewable energy systems, carbon storage and climate‑adaptive planning, and examines climate governance and justice.
selectedCourses.contribution: provides the climate science whose consequences the moral argument is about
selectedCourses.descriptionRead: Focuses on drivers and impacts of anthropogenic climate change on sea level, ocean acidification, ecology and society. Discusses adaptation and mitigation solutions, including renewable energy systems, carbon storage and climate‑adaptive planning, and examines climate governance and justice.

selectedCourses.name: Life Cycle Analysis & Circular Economy
selectedCourses.evidenceRead: Develops life-cycle approaches to evaluating products, processes and services within a circular economy. Students examine environmental, social and health consequences from resource extraction to disposal or reuse, together with costs, revenues and management strategies. Three preliminary projects develop different parts or forms of life-cycle analysis, followed by a project that integrates the stages into a full product or process assessment.
selectedCourses.officialDescriptionRead: Teaches evaluation of environmental impacts of products, processes and services throughout their lifecycle. Emphasises strategic planning for a circular economy through hands‑on learning.
selectedCourses.contribution: analyses life-cycle assessment and circular-economy design as concrete sustainability practice
selectedCourses.descriptionRead: Teaches evaluation of environmental impacts of products, processes and services throughout their lifecycle. Emphasises strategic planning for a circular economy through hands‑on learning.

selectedCourses.name: Calling Bullshit
selectedCourses.evidenceRead: Examines misinformation through philosophy, history, psychology and practical information evaluation. Students distinguish misleading discourse from related concepts, investigate cognitive and social vulnerabilities, and analyze pseudoscience, statistical misrepresentation and reasoning errors. Fact-checking, deepfake production and response exercises develop recognition and intervention skills. Projects map a misinformation narrative's actors and circulation and produce a research-grounded myth-debunking video with an external interview.
selectedCourses.officialDescriptionRead: Develops skills to recognise and handle misinformation. Discusses cognitive biases and detection methods, distinguishes real from fake experts, and includes case studies and a video project tackling a misinformation topic.
selectedCourses.contribution: trains systematic detection of misinformation, pseudoscience and statistical manipulation and the assessment of scientific credibility
selectedCourses.descriptionRead: Develops skills to recognise and handle misinformation. Discusses cognitive biases and detection methods, distinguishes real from fake experts, and includes case studies and a video project tackling a misinformation topic.

selectedCourses.name: Renewable System Design
selectedCourses.evidenceRead: Teaches assessment of energy usage patterns and strategies for reducing consumption or transitioning to cleaner energy. Explores solar, wind and bioenergy solutions and includes technical and economic analysis; students deliver a report and presentation to a partner company.
selectedCourses.officialDescriptionRead: Teaches assessment of energy usage patterns and strategies for reducing consumption or transitioning to cleaner energy. Explores solar, wind and bioenergy solutions and includes technical and economic analysis; students deliver a report and presentation to a partner company.
selectedCourses.contribution: requires the design of renewable systems, grounding normative debate in technical feasibility
selectedCourses.descriptionRead: Teaches assessment of energy usage patterns and strategies for reducing consumption or transitioning to cleaner energy. Explores solar, wind and bioenergy solutions and includes technical and economic analysis; students deliver a report and presentation to a partner company.

selectedCourses.name: Research in a Sustainable Delta
selectedCourses.evidenceRead: Provides a research-project setting for sustainability questions supplied by organizations and companies in the Zeeland delta. Small teams work with an external advisor to review literature, formulate a research question, plan and execute an investigation, and develop a final product, design or report. The substantive topic and practical techniques depend on the partner project; the common focus is an evidence-based research process and engagement with external stakeholders.
selectedCourses.officialDescriptionRead: In this project course you will work in small teams of two or three students on a research problem relevant for sustainability in the broadest sense. We are looking for collaborations with local companies and other institutions. The research questions are supplied by a regional institution or company that is active in areas related to sustainability in the broadest sense. In this way it is guaranteed that the research projects are indeed relevant for the Zeeland delta. Furthermore, students will have access to expertise and/or facilities of the external partner, which will broaden their perspective. Usually, there will be one person affiliated with the external partner organization involved with a project team as external advisor
selectedCourses.contribution: Small teams investigate partner-defined sustainability problems using literature review, research design and a final product or report. This is collaborative applied research, not an individual philosophical thesis; the project topic is not predetermined.
selectedCourses.descriptionRead: In this project course you will work in small teams of two or three students on a research problem relevant for sustainability in the broadest sense. We are looking for collaborations with local companies and other institutions. The research questions are supplied by a regional institution or company that is active in areas related to sustainability in the broadest sense. In this way it is guaranteed that the research projects are indeed relevant for the Zeeland delta. selectedCourses.name: Modern History
selectedCourses.evidenceRead: Surveys economic, political and cultural developments from 1815 to the present while questioning the meaning and periodization of modernity. Students examine industrialization, political ideologies, nationalism, imperialism, migration, world wars, revolution, decolonization, the Cold War and globalization. Historical research and essays connect specific questions to evidence. A group project analyzes historical visions of the future as products of their own contexts and compares them with subsequent developments.
selectedCourses.officialDescriptionRead: Provides a chronological overview of history from 1815 to the present. Discusses industrialisation, popular sovereignty and national self‑determination, and covers major economic, political and cultural developments including revolutions, world wars and the fall of communism.
selectedCourses.contribution: gives the chronological account of the modern period in which popular sovereignty, Marxism, socialism and liberal political ideals took shape
selectedCourses.descriptionRead: Provides a chronological overview of history from 1815 to the present. Discusses industrialisation, popular sovereignty and national self‑determination, and covers major economic, political and cultural developments including revolutions, world wars and the fall of communism.

selectedCourses.name: Histories of Gender
selectedCourses.evidenceRead: Studies gendered histories and lives in North America from the nineteenth century to the present, centering storytelling and intersectionality. Queer and heteronormative narratives connect slavery, family, sexuality, health, incarceration and contemporary backlash to resistance and activism. Students interpret primary sources and scholarship, interview older queer people, contribute to the Walking with Pride activist artwork, and conduct an original research project in a chosen format.
selectedCourses.officialDescriptionRead: Explores lives of ordinary people through the lens of gender from the 19th to 21st centuries. Uses storytelling across cultural forms; topics include slavery, mid‑20th‑century life, conversion therapy, queer cinema and banned books; engages with projects like Walking With Pride.
selectedCourses.contribution: examines the body, lived experience and power through the histories of gender, drawing on hooks and Crenshaw
selectedCourses.descriptionRead: Studies gender, storytelling and marginalised lives in the nineteenth- to twenty-first-century American context. Students examine slavery, community activism, representation and lived experience, using sources and projects that connect historical interpretation with contemporary questions.

sharedDescriptionProvenance.reviewNote: Compared with the current selected workbook field. Retained the existing description as a faithful account; updated its source provenance.

selectedCourses.name: Human Rights: Law & Philosophy
selectedCourses.evidenceRead: Studies human rights both as positive law and as philosophical claims. Students examine the UDHR, European and UN protection systems, monitoring institutions and landmark cases alongside natural law, natural rights, legal positivism and critiques of universality. Historical and philosophical texts frame debates about dignity, life and reproductive rights, punishment, religious freedom, expression and democracy. Close engagement with legal and philosophical arguments supports independent moral positions.
selectedCourses.officialDescriptionRead: Offers a legal, historical and philosophical approach to human rights. Studies classical and modern philosophers, traces the rise of human rights, examines the US Bill of Rights and the French Declaration, and discusses human rights treaties.
selectedCourses.contribution: studies human rights legally, historically and philosophically, from the classical declarations to contemporary treaties
selectedCourses.descriptionRead: Offers a legal, historical and philosophical approach to human rights. Studies classical and modern philosophers, traces the rise of human rights, examines the US Bill of Rights and the French Declaration, and discusses human rights treaties.

selectedCourses.name: Introduction to Western Philosophy
selectedCourses.evidenceRead: Introduces major philosophical questions through close study of arguments from ancient Greek thought to contemporary philosophy, with a related Buddhist perspective on the self. Students examine knowledge, ethics, God, mind and consciousness, freedom, identity, time and meaning. Historical texts and contemporary debates, including AI consciousness and concepts of race and gender, develop the ability to reconstruct, evaluate and formulate philosophical arguments in focused essays.
selectedCourses.officialDescriptionRead: Introduces central themes from Western philosophy over 2,500 years. Encourages inquiry into the significance of philosophical issues and their relation to other disciplines and teaches theoretical methods used by philosophers.
selectedCourses.contribution: provides the systematic introduction to Western philosophical questions, arguments and traditions on which the later philosophical work depends
selectedCourses.descriptionRead: Introduces central themes from Western philosophy over 2,500 years. Encourages inquiry into the significance of philosophical issues and their relation to other disciplines and teaches theoretical methods used by philosophers.

selectedCourses.name: Ethics
selectedCourses.evidenceRead: Studies moral reasoning through historical and contemporary ethical theories and close philosophical reading. Utilitarianism, consequentialism, Kantian ethics, virtue ethics, contractarianism and feminist ethics lead into Nietzsche's genealogy, Murdoch's account of goodness and Nagel's treatments of value, perspective, death and meaning. Reflection and research essays require interpretation, argument evaluation and an independent position on ethical theory or a practical ethical problem.
selectedCourses.officialDescriptionRead: Explores theories of moral reasoning—virtue ethics, deontology, utilitarianism—and discusses moral knowledge, motivation, responsibility and the relation between happiness and pleasure. Applies theories to practical issues such as animal rights, privacy, future generations, war, punishment, disability and equality.
selectedCourses.contribution: Develops utilitarian, Kantian, virtue, contractarian and feminist ethics through close reading, argument evaluation and independent essays. Directly supplies moral-theory foundations; environmental topics and their weight are not assumed from an older syllabus.
selectedCourses.descriptionRead: Ethics examines moral reasoning through historical and contemporary theories and close philosophical reading. Students study utilitarianism, Kantian ethics, virtue ethics, contractarianism and feminist ethics, alongside Nietzsche, Murdoch and Nagel. Reflection and research essays develop interpretation, argument evaluation and an independent position on ethical theory or a practical ethical problem.

selectedCourses.name: Philosophy of Mind
selectedCourses.evidenceRead: Examines minds, selves and conscious experience through historical and contemporary philosophy. Personal identity and self-knowledge are considered alongside Buddhist accounts and neuropsychological cases. Behaviourism, physicalism, functionalism and their critics frame the mind-body problem. Later inquiries address machine consciousness, virtual worlds, dreaming, perception, transformative experience and the value of experience. Essays develop independent philosophical interpretations and arguments.
selectedCourses.officialDescriptionRead: Examines historical and modern work on the philosophy of mind. Discusses Descartes’ dualism, the nature of consciousness, AI and animal minds, personal identity, transformative experiences and the influence of technology on experience.
selectedCourses.contribution: examines consciousness, personal identity, the mind-body problem and machine consciousness as philosophical problems
selectedCourses.descriptionRead: Examines historical and modern work on the philosophy of mind. Discusses Descartes’ dualism, the nature of consciousness, AI and animal minds, personal identity, transformative experiences and the influence of technology on experience.

selectedCourses.name: Philosophy of Emotion
selectedCourses.evidenceRead: Examines what emotions are and how they shape knowledge, decision-making, ethics, social life and politics. Feeling, cognitive and perceptual theories are compared with historical, phenomenological and contemporary accounts. Love, fear, grief, moods and political anger provide focused cases, alongside emotions in art and their changing relation to time. Students analyze texts and emotional vignettes and develop an independent philosophical paper or a project combining argument with creative work.
selectedCourses.officialDescriptionRead: Explores emotions from a philosophical perspective. Discusses nature and rationality of emotions, their role in ethics and art, and draws on historical and contemporary sources.
selectedCourses.contribution: analyses emotion and affect philosophically, including their relation to rationality, value and well-being
selectedCourses.descriptionRead: Explores emotions from a philosophical perspective. Discusses nature and rationality of emotions, their role in ethics and art, and draws on historical and contemporary sources.

selectedCourses.name: Free Will, Time & the Self
selectedCourses.evidenceRead: Explores free will and agency in relation to time and the self. Historical Greek and Indian perspectives introduce debates about fatalism, determinism, compatibility and moral responsibility; later topics include scientific challenges, addiction, luck and agency in games. The second part examines the reality and experience of time, physics and temporal asymmetries, then developing research linking time, action and selfhood. Essays require close source analysis and an independent argument.
selectedCourses.officialDescriptionRead: Investigates concepts of free will, the role of luck and openness of the future. Explores relations between free will, time and the self across multiple modules and contemporary debates.
selectedCourses.contribution: treats free will, time, agency and the self as advanced metaphysical problems
selectedCourses.descriptionRead: Investigates concepts of free will, the role of luck and openness of the future. Explores relations between free will, time and the self across multiple modules and contemporary debates.

selectedCourses.name: Introduction to Political Philosophy
selectedCourses.evidenceRead: Surveys political thought from classical antiquity to contemporary debates, including European and non-European thinkers. Students examine views of human nature, society, rights and authority in their historical contexts and compare their proposed solutions with current political problems. Close study of original texts, an individual essay and a group project developing a coherent political philosophy connect historical interpretation to normative argument.
selectedCourses.officialDescriptionRead: Introduces political philosophy. Examines concepts such as authority, freedom, equality, democracy, human rights, pluralism, multiculturalism, poverty and environmental issues through classical and contemporary texts. Emphasises essay writing and presentations.
selectedCourses.contribution: Studies European and non-European political thought, human nature, society, rights and authority through original texts, essays and a group political-philosophy project. Directly supports normative political inquiry.
selectedCourses.descriptionRead: Introduction to Political Philosophy examines political thought from classical antiquity to contemporary debates, including European and non-European thinkers. Students study views of human nature, society, rights and authority in historical context and compare their arguments with current political problems. Original texts, an essay and a group project develop interpretation and normative argument.

selectedCourses.name: Qualitative Research Methodology
selectedCourses.evidenceRead: Develops qualitative inquiry from research design and preparation through data collection, management, analysis and dissemination. Students examine methodological foundations, ethics, positionality and reflexivity alongside interviews, focus groups, ethnography, documentary and visual approaches. Coding, thematic interpretation and NVivo support analysis. Research teams formulate a question, collect and analyze qualitative evidence, and report their methodological decisions, findings and limitations in staged assignments.
selectedCourses.officialDescriptionRead: Introduces qualitative research methodology. Covers designing questions, interpreting meaning and conducting small team projects, while reflecting on complexity and power dynamics in social research.
selectedCourses.contribution: Develops qualitative research design, ethics, positionality, interviews, ethnography and documentary or visual approaches, with coding and interpretation. Complements philosophical questions about knowledge with an actual empirical inquiry method; it is not a systematic epistemology course.
selectedCourses.descriptionRead: Introduces qualitative research methodology. Covers designing questions, interpreting meaning and conducting small team projects, while reflecting on complexity and power dynamics in social research.

selectedCourses.name: Modern Sociology
selectedCourses.evidenceRead: Examines twentieth-century and contemporary social theory alongside critical accounts of modernity, colonialism and disciplinary exclusion. Functionalism, critical theory, Black feminist thought, phenomenology, symbolic interactionism and Bourdieu's work are read with postcolonial, decolonial and Indigenous perspectives. Students compare theories and apply them to empirical cases, including visual material. An individual research paper develops a theoretically grounded interpretation of a selected social phenomenon.
selectedCourses.officialDescriptionRead: Examines the trajectory of sociology within the culture of imperialism and colonial responses. Studies leading social theories and debates about modernity and critically engages with sociological discourses.
selectedCourses.contribution: traces the development of sociology and social theory through modernity, imperialism and colonial responses
selectedCourses.descriptionRead: Examines the trajectory of sociology within the culture of imperialism and colonial responses. Studies leading social theories and debates about modernity and critically engages with sociological discourses.

selectedCourses.name: Social Movements & Environmental Justice
selectedCourses.evidenceRead: Focuses on social movement theories and environmental justice. Uses case studies from the Environmental Justice Atlas and integrates perspectives such as feminism, anti‑colonialism, degrowth and environmental peacebuilding to encourage civic engagement.

selectedCourses.name: Higher Order Functions
selectedCourses.evidenceRead: Deepens understanding of neuroanatomy, neurophysiology and the experimental study of higher cognitive functions. Students examine attention, memory, emotion, cognitive control, social cognition, pain and consciousness, connecting brain function and dysfunction to behaviour. An attentional-blink experiment provides direct engagement with empirical work. A team research proposal requires literature analysis, a feasible experimental design and ethical reflection, supported by peer review.
selectedCourses.officialDescriptionRead: Deepens understanding of neurophysiology and neuroanatomy. Explores higher‑level cognitive functions—memory, emotion, social cognition, executive functioning and language—and engages with current research while designing experiments.
selectedCourses.contribution: deepens the study of memory, attention, executive function and cognitive control that philosophy of mind treats conceptually
selectedCourses.descriptionRead: Higher Order Functions deepens knowledge of neurophysiology, neuroanatomy and experimental cognitive neuroscience. An attentional-blink experiment and a team research proposal develop engagement with empirical research, experimental design and ethical reflection.

selectedCourses.name: Psycholinguistics
selectedCourses.evidenceRead: Psycholinguistics is the study of the neurobiological and psychological factors that enable us to acquire, use, and understand language. Modern research draws on cognitive psychology, neuroscience, and computer science to investigate how language is processed. The course focuses primarily, though not exclusively, on the neuroscience of language. Students examine theoretical and experimental issues in speech production and comprehension, language impairments, the relationship between thought and language, and the evolution and acquisition of language. They also gain hands-on experience with experimental approaches to the study of language and develop an understanding of human linguistic capacity as a subject of multidisciplinary research. Topics covered: What is language? Evolutionary aspects of language and animal communication; language and thought; aphasia; language acquisition; bilingualism; speech comprehension; semantics; reading and dyslexia; speech production.

selectedCourses.name: Introduction to Brain & Behavior
selectedCourses.evidenceRead: Introduces psychological and neuroscientific explanations of behaviour and mental processes. Students study neural signalling, brain anatomy and development, learning, intelligence, personality, social influence, mental disorders and treatments. Several sessions introduce behavioural, imaging and electrophysiological approaches to neuroscience and their combined use. Interdisciplinary research-article and case analysis connects psychological processes to neural mechanisms and clinical questions.
selectedCourses.officialDescriptionRead: Explores why people behave as they do and how brain injuries affect mental processes. Discusses nature and nurture, introduces brain anatomy and psychological theories, and provides a gateway to cognitive science and clinical psychology.
selectedCourses.contribution: provides the foundational account of brain and behaviour that the programme's later mind and language courses build on
selectedCourses.descriptionRead: Explores why people behave as they do and how brain injuries affect mental processes. Discusses nature and nurture, introduces brain anatomy and psychological theories, and provides a gateway to cognitive science and clinical psychology.

selectedCourses.name: The Art of Rhetorical Communication
selectedCourses.evidenceRead: Teaches rhetorical analysis and persuasive communication through classical history, theory and practice. Students study Greek and Roman rhetoric, the five canons, types of discourse, persuasive appeals, argumentation and fallacies. Written exercises, debates and public speeches develop invention, arrangement, style, memory and delivery. An applied project creates narrative and storytelling material for an immersive educational setting concerned with Zeeland's climate and community.
selectedCourses.officialDescriptionRead: Teaches how to craft persuasive messages, influence opinions, inspire action and connect people. Draws on historical communicators from Aristotle to Barack Obama and applies stylistic techniques to students’ own writing and speaking.
selectedCourses.contribution: analyses rhetorical argument through ethos, pathos and logos and requires students to construct and evaluate persuasive cases
selectedCourses.descriptionRead: The Art of Rhetorical Communication develops rhetorical analysis, academic writing and oral presentation. Students examine classical Western roots and the canons of rhetoric, and learn to construct, organise and support persuasive arguments. Historical and contemporary examples connect rhetorical theory with practical communication.

selectedCourses.name: Style & Meaning
selectedCourses.evidenceRead: Studies how linguistic choices produce meaning and interpretive effects, principally in literary texts but also in nonfiction. Students connect linguistic description to interpretation across grammar, discourse and cognition. Stylistic frameworks address foregrounding, dialogue, narration, modality, transitivity, deixis, schemas, construal and text worlds. Frequent analysis exercises lead to an original, research-supported stylistic analysis of a selected text.
selectedCourses.officialDescriptionRead: Explores how linguistic choices inform meaning and interpretation in literary and non-fiction contexts. Introduces theoretical frameworks for close reading and addresses power dynamics, obligation, uncertainty and ideological undertones in language.
selectedCourses.contribution: develops close stylistic reading, showing how linguistic choices create meaning and carry ideological weight

selectedCourses.name: Persuasive Communication

Students study coactive persuasion, framing, argumentation, cognitive shortcuts and verbal and nonverbal communication. Projects with the Delta Climate Centre and Vlissingen municipality develop communication encouraging sustainable and circular lifestyles. An individual research paper evaluates selected persuasion tools through literature review, field research diaries and reflective analysis of their use.

Museums, exhibitions, curatorial choices and Eurocentric narratives are treated critically. An independently researched paper develops a focused art-historical question, methods and evidence-based argument.

conceptJudgments: The closest response has eight directly philosophical/legal-political/AI-ethical courses plus formal logic, supplemented by actual social theory, historical interpretation, close reading, rhetoric and empirical cognition. It responds materially to philosophical inquiry rather than being general human-science breadth. Dedicated epistemology, philosophy of science, Enlightenment and philosopher-specific seminars remain gaps. No full specialist equivalence is claimed.

Technology direction changes ten courses/75EC from the closest: actual data analysis, machine learning, neural networks, relational information, calculus and media technologies implement investigation of AI/information and mediation. These are complementary technical and interpretive studies, not a philosophy-of-information syllabus. Ethics, mind, metaphysics, emotion and human rights retain the philosophical organising spine. Programme-level response is justified by direct technology and interdisciplinary-philosophy interests 780/785 and the formal technology/media components.

Environmental direction changes13courses/97.5EC from closest and15/112.5EC from technology. Moral/political philosophy, human rights and social theory organise the normative inquiry; actual climate, ecosystems, resource technology, lifecycle assessment, governance, environmental justice and environmental communication supply its specific objects, constraints and practices. Laboratory and technical courses are material environmental knowledge, not themselves ethical argument. A full philosophy degree remains distinct. Eligible sustainability interest782 and Moral Philosophy and Environmental Practice support this direction; no imagined engineering interest is introduced.

No fourth direction: all15 direct interests have substantive ownership in the closest or the two distinct evidenced candidates. Medical/economic philosophical applications in785 do not establish a separate mandatory UCR medical/economic curriculum. Examples and post-degree outcomes cannot generate alternatives.
alignmentFinding: Every22 external components and47 selected identities assessed independently. Formal logic now reflects the actual propositional/quantified logic and proofs; Ethics contributes moral theory without the old environmental-case claim; metaphysics, bodies/gender and language/mind relationships retain explicit disciplinary limits. History/social theory, media, political philosophy and mind alignments address identifiable primary subjects; unmatched epistemology, philosophy of science, Enlightenment, Dutch philosophical tradition, advanced philosopher/information seminars, practice, open minor and thesis remain visible. Optional independent research15EC now explicitly anchors to the thesis via researchComponentId, outside every scheduled180EC.
alignments: Human Conditions and Philosophy of Mind both take the philosophical analysis of what it is to be human as their primary subject: consciousness, personal identity and the limits of naturalistic explanation.

Both address moral philosophy and ethical reasoning. UCR provides sustained study of moral theories and independent argument; the Erasmus course explicitly connects moral philosophy with environmental practice.
Both address metaphysical questions. UCR studies free will, agency, time and selfhood through historical and contemporary arguments; it does not reproduce a systematic continental-metaphysics course.

Contemporary Thought of Technology and AI Ethics both examine technology philosophically. UCR's course concentrates that examination on artificial intelligence, fairness, alignment and human flourishing.

Theoretical Analytic Philosophy is a dedicated survey of analytic method and its central problems. No single UCR course occupies that role; the material is spread across Philosophy of Mind, Free Will, Time & the Self and Logic & Discrete Mathematics, so the component is left unmatched rather than forced onto one of them.

What Can We Know? is a systematic epistemology course running from antiquity to the modern age. UCR offers no epistemology course, and Introduction to Western Philosophy — which touches these questions — is the counterpart of the Rotterdam introduction rather than of this one.
Filosofie in Nederland studies the Dutch philosophical tradition specifically. UCR has no counterpart and none is manufactured.

Both develop formal logical reasoning. UCR explicitly teaches propositional and quantified logic, proof, sets and induction, with additional mathematical and game-modelling applications; it does not reproduce the complete philosophical-logic course.

Philosophy of Science is a dedicated course on scientific knowledge, method and explanation. UCR has no philosophy-of-science course. Calling Bullshit trains the evaluation of evidence and scientific credibility but is a critical-thinking course rather than a philosophical treatment of science, so the component is left unmatched.

Filosofie in de Praktijk places philosophical skills in professional practice. UCR's Personal & Professional Development serves a different purpose — personal formation and academic-skills development, without the disciplinary content — so the component is recorded as unmatched rather than equated with it.

Historisering van het Wereldbeeld and Modern History both study how worldviews were historically formed and transformed; the UCR course does so through the political and intellectual history of the modern period from 1815.
Geschiedenis, Maatschappij en Individu and Modern Sociology both examine the relation between society and the individual through social theory and the history of modernity.

Both address bodies, experience and power. UCR studies these through North American gender histories, intersectionality and primary-source research; it is a partial historical relationship to the philosophical component.

Politics and Critique and Introduction to Political Philosophy are both the programme's political-philosophy component, examining political authority, society and critique through influential thinkers.

Enlightenment is a dedicated study of Enlightenment philosophy. Modern History begins in 1815 and is already the counterpart of Historisering van het Wereldbeeld, so no UCR course covers this period philosophically and the gap is preserved.

Taal en Geest and Psycholinguistics both address the relation between language and mind. The Rotterdam course does so philosophically and the UCR course through the neurobiological and psychological study of language acquisition, production and comprehension; the primary subject is the same.

Wittgenstein is a dedicated advanced seminar on one philosopher and his work on language, logic and meaning. UCR addresses some related questions in broader philosophy and language courses but offers no dedicated Wittgenstein or philosophy-of-language course, so the component remains unmatched.

Philosophy of Art, Media & Technology and Introduction to Film & Media share art, media and technology as their subject, including how media technologies shape perception and cultural production; the UCR course is an analytical rather than a philosophical treatment.

Philosophies of Information and Computation treats information and computation as philosophical subjects. UCR offers technical computing, formal logic and AI-ethics courses, but none centres on the philosophy of information and computation, so the component remains unmatched rather than being equated with applied technical study.

The Rotterdam programme reserves 15 EC of genuine non-philosophy profiling space as a minor or exchange period. UCR programmes are composed entirely of 7.5-EC courses and have no equivalent reserved block, so the space is shown as it stands.
The Bachelor Thesis Filosofie is a 15-EC supervised independent philosophical study. None of the 24 scheduled UCR courses is a thesis, so the component is recorded as unmatched.
